checks: Choose an interior point of the old trace on a positive fiber and a closed ball of positive radius around that point within the fiber. The continuous normal stays nonzero near the old normal. The signed distance from the ball center to each cutting plane is continuous in the normal and level; when that distance is at most half the ball radius, all sections have a uniform positive (d−1)-volume lower bound, including counting measure one in d=1.

The ambient level shift equals the fiber level shift because the base remains fixed. Slice integration divides by the continuous normal norm, which is bounded above and away from zero near the old cut. The mass difference of the nested closed caps is at least a positive constant times the level increase as long as both cutting levels stay near the old one. Their boundaries are fiber-volume null. Other fibers only increase this loss and need not be proper or separately differentiable.

For a point in the strict interior of H, a small positive threshold increase below its positive margin preserves containment and strictly reduces mass. On the boundary at a different point, take v=Y′−Y and N_t=N+t v. All sufficiently small signed t give genuine through-Y halfspaces, whose masses are at least Q by actual attainment. Two-sided differentiability at this local minimum gives Q+o(t); no derivative at Y′ is invoked.

The threshold of the cap through Y′ at N_t exceeds the through-Y threshold by t||v||² because N·v=0. Both thresholds converge to the old one. The uniform strip pays a positive multiple of t||v||² and strictly beats the o(t) term for t>0 sufficiently small. Y itself belongs to H and has depth Q, proving the asserted equality as an ambient statement.

overlap.comparison: Sections 2–3 give the same contact conclusion (and the centroid identity) under positive coarea and zero (d−1)-measure on every nonproper trace. The added scope is real: in d=1, use the centrally symmetric fibers [−2,0], [−1,1], [0,2] at bases −1,0,1 and the minimizing cap x≥0 through the origin. All nearby through-origin nonvertical caps have half the mass by reflection, so the required directional derivatives exist. The two endpoint traces are supporting singletons of positive counting measure, so the accepted sufficient trace hypothesis fails.
